name: Fanesca
history: Fanesca is Ecuador's Holy Week soup, traditionally combining salt cod, squash, milk and a symbolic variety of grains and pulses. Families prepare it communally and finish each bowl with colourful garnishes.
servingSuggestions: Garnish with hard-boiled egg, fried plantain, cheese, parsley and small empanadas.
ingredients: Salt cod – 500 g, soaked and drained
Cooked lentils, beans and chickpeas – 250 g each
Cooked maize and peas – 200 g each
Cumin, achiote, cheese and cream – as needed
instructions: Soak salt cod overnight, changing the water several times; poach gently in milk and flake, checking for bones.
Cook onion, garlic, achiote and cumin, then stir in squash purée and ground peanuts.
Add the poaching milk and all cooked grains and pulses; simmer slowly for 25 minutes.
Fold in most of the cod, cheese and a little cream without breaking the beans.
Adjust thickness and salt carefully, then add the remaining cod and garnishes.

name: Cepelinai
history: Cepelinai are Lithuania's zeppelin-shaped potato dumplings, usually filled with seasoned pork and served with bacon-onion sauce and sour cream. A mix of raw and cooked potato gives the casing structure.
servingSuggestions: Serve hot with sour cream, crisp bacon and onions.
ingredients: Marjoram, salt and black pepper – to taste
instructions: Grate raw potatoes finely, squeeze very dry in cloth and reserve the settled starch from the liquid.
Mix raw potato, mashed potato, reserved starch and salt into a mouldable dough.
Season pork with onion, marjoram, salt and pepper and form eight small oval portions.
Wrap each filling completely in potato dough and lower into gently simmering salted water.
Cook for 25–30 minutes, then serve with fried bacon, onion and sour cream.

name: Kedjenou
history: Kedjenou is an Ivorian chicken stew cooked in a tightly sealed pot with vegetables and almost no added liquid. Shaking rather than stirring preserves the concentrated juices.
servingSuggestions: Serve with attiéké, rice or boiled plantain.
ingredients: Scotch bonnet, thyme, salt and pepper – to taste
instructions: Season chicken with ginger, garlic, thyme, salt and pepper.
Layer chicken, tomato, onion, aubergine, pepper and whole Scotch bonnet in a heavy pot.
Cover tightly and cook over low heat without adding water; shake the pot every 10 minutes.
After about 55 minutes, check that the chicken is tender and safely cooked through.
Remove the whole chilli for gentler heat and reduce uncovered briefly only if necessary.

name: Kongguksu
history: Kongguksu is a Korean summer noodle bowl in a chilled, savoury soy-bean broth. Blended beans and sesame create a naturally creamy texture without dairy.
servingSuggestions: Serve very cold with cucumber, tomato, sesame and optional ice cubes.
instructions: Boil soaked soybeans until just tender, 12–15 minutes, then cool and rub away loose skins.
Blend beans with sesame, pine nuts, salt and cold water until completely smooth; strain if desired.
Chill the broth for at least 30 minutes and adjust salt only when cold.
Cook noodles, rinse repeatedly under cold water and drain thoroughly.
Divide noodles into bowls, pour over soy broth and add cucumber and tomato.

name: Hiyashi chūka
history: Hiyashi chūka is a colourful Japanese summer dish of chilled ramen noodles arranged with fine strips of egg, cucumber, tomato and protein, then dressed with a bright soy-vinegar sauce.
servingSuggestions: Serve cold with Japanese mustard and toasted sesame.
ingredients: Cooked chicken or ham – 200 g, shredded
Sesame oil, sugar, ginger and sesame seeds – for dressing
instructions: Whisk soy, vinegar, sesame oil, sugar and grated ginger until the sugar dissolves; chill.
Cook thin omelettes from the eggs, cool and slice into fine strips.
Boil noodles until springy, rinse very well in cold water and drain.
Arrange noodles in shallow bowls and place cucumber, tomato, egg and chicken in separate bands.
Spoon over the chilled dressing just before eating.

name: Rfissa
history: Rfissa is a Moroccan celebratory platter of shredded msemen or trid pastry soaked with aromatic chicken, lentil and fenugreek broth. Ras el hanout and saffron perfume the sauce.
servingSuggestions: Pile the pastry on a wide platter, spoon over broth and arrange chicken and lentils on top.
ingredients: Saffron and ground ginger – to taste
Olive oil, butter, coriander, salt and pepper – as needed
instructions: Marinate chicken with onion, spices, oil, salt and pepper for 30 minutes.
Cook chicken and onions in a covered pot, adding water gradually to form a rich broth.
Add lentils and drained fenugreek and simmer until tender; remove chicken when safely cooked.
Steam or warm the flatbreads and tear them into ribbons on a large platter.
Moisten bread generously with hot broth and top with lentils, onions and chicken.

name: Ochazuke
history: Ochazuke is a light Japanese bowl made by pouring hot green tea or dashi over cooked rice. Small savoury toppings turn leftover rice into a soothing quick meal.
servingSuggestions: Offer extra nori, wasabi and rice crackers so each bowl can be adjusted at the table.
ingredients: Green tea or light dashi – 500 ml, hot
instructions: Warm the rice thoroughly and divide it between two deep bowls.
Season the salmon lightly and place it over the rice with nori and spring onion.
Pour very hot tea or dashi around the rice until partly submerged.
Finish with rice crackers and sesame and eat immediately before the crackers soften.

name: Eromba
history: Eromba is a Manipuri mash of boiled vegetables, chillies and fermented fish, valued for its smoky heat and deep umami. Seasonal greens and herbs vary by household.
servingSuggestions: Serve with steamed rice and a mild vegetable side.
ingredients: Fresh or dried chillies – to taste
instructions: Boil potatoes, bamboo shoots and beans separately until tender and drain well.
Roast or boil the chillies and fermented fish until aromatic and fully heated.
Mash potatoes with fermented fish and chillies to a coarse paste.
Fold in chopped vegetables, onion, coriander and salt without making the mixture smooth.
Rest for five minutes so the flavours combine, then serve warm.

name: Pepián
history: Pepián is one of Guatemala's foundational recados: a thick stew whose sauce is built from charred tomatoes, chillies, pumpkin seeds, sesame and toasted spices.
servingSuggestions: Serve with rice, warm corn tortillas and chopped coriander.
ingredients: Dried guajillo and ancho chillies – 3 each
Cinnamon, allspice, coriander seed, onion and garlic – as needed
instructions: Toast pumpkin seeds, sesame, spices and tortillas separately until fragrant without burning.
Char tomatoes, tomatillos, onion, garlic and seeded chillies on a dry pan.
Blend all toasted ingredients with stock into a smooth, thick sauce.
Brown chicken, pour over the sauce and enough stock to loosen, then simmer covered.
Cook until chicken is tender and safe, stirring often as the seed sauce thickens.

name: Nam khao
history: Nam khao is a Lao crispy rice salad made by frying coconut-red-curry rice balls, then breaking them into crunchy fragments with herbs, lime, peanuts and fermented sausage.
servingSuggestions: Spoon into lettuce leaves with extra herbs, chilli and lime.
ingredients: Som moo fermented pork or cooked sour sausage – 200 g
Mint, coriander, spring onion, fish sauce and chilli – as needed
instructions: Mix rice with curry paste, coconut, egg and salt; compress into firm balls.
Deep-fry at 175°C until dark golden and crisp, then drain and cool slightly.
Break rice balls into small crunchy pieces in a wide bowl.
Add sliced sausage, lime, fish sauce, peanuts, herbs, spring onion and chilli.
Toss just before serving so some rice remains crisp.
